author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Under the Seventh Scratch
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The seventh scratch was not hidden.

That was what made the whole affair faintly embarrassing. For months we'd treated it like a secret carved by a clever ancestor. It ran down the lowest stone beneath Lanternwell's western arch, plain enough to see once Tamsin cleaned away the moss.

"Maintenance mark," she said.

Maui leaned closer. "Could still be a very dramatic maintenance mark."

"Only to someone who has never paid a mason."

Fen laughed.

The preliminary survey had located a shallow inspection hatch beneath the arch. It was not a Threadway, and opening it would not take us to another world. It led to the dry upper section of the old drainage passage, separated by a locked flood barrier from the lower channel that remained sealed after the Closed Bells.

We could inspect the upper section, but only under conditions.

Danse tested the air. Toph checked movement through the foundation. Tamsin installed temporary supports and marked how much weight the floor could bear. Neri brought the old service drawings. Edda checked the stair opening and, when she found it inaccessible to some of the people involved, insisted that the observations be recorded in a format everyone could review afterward.

Nobody was allowed down alone.

Maui looked at the checklist.

"All of this to look at a hole?"

"All of this so we can come back out of it," I said.

He grinned, but he didn't argue.

The key around my neck fit the upper hatch. I turned it only after Fen confirmed the tide was falling and Danse had read out the test results. The lock resisted, then gave with a heavy click.

The hatch opened onto a narrow flight of stone steps.

Cool air rose from below. It smelled of old water, mineral dust, and the faint metal tang of a place that hadn't been properly ventilated in years.

I felt an irrational rush of fear.

Maui noticed.

"We can stop," he said.

"I know."

"Would you like to?"

I looked at the lantern in my hand, then at the safety rope tied to the anchored ring.

"Not yet."

We descended with Tamsin. Danse remained above, monitoring the line, while Toph kept contact with the stone foundation and Fen watched the water level from the safe opening.

The chamber was smaller than I'd imagined.

No treasure. No secret doorway to a lover. No altar with my name written in gold.

There were shallow channels cut into the floor, iron brackets for a removable gate, and two narrow recesses where maintenance tools had once been stored. Old chalk marks showed measured water heights. One wall held a set of notches that matched the seventh scratch above.

Maui stared around.

"That's it?"

"That's a great deal of history," Tamsin said.

I ran my light over the brackets. One was bent. The stone around it had been patched with material of a different color.

"Someone repaired this after the sealing," I said.

Tamsin examined the mortar.

"Maybe. We'll take a sample from the loose edge and compare it with the documented work orders. No guessing."

There was a narrow passage beyond the chamber, ending in the sealed flood barrier. Water sounded faintly on the other side, not moving freely but pressing and withdrawing with the tide.

The sound reminded me of a person breathing through a closed door.

Maui moved toward it.

Tamsin raised a hand.

"Stop at the yellow mark."

He stopped.

He looked irritated at first, then afraid. I understood the feeling. The whole point of his old stories had been that he could reach what other people could not. Here was a door with water behind it, and the right thing to do was stand back.

"Do you think people were trapped here?" he asked.

"We don't know whether anyone stood in this chamber," I said. "We know travel was restricted elsewhere. The records are still incomplete."

He nodded.

I checked the brass key in my hand. It had opened a maintenance hatch, nothing more.

Part of me wanted that to be disappointing.

Instead I felt free.

The key did not appoint me keeper of the valley. It did not tell me whom to love, where to live, or which doors I had to walk through. It was a tool, made by people who had needed access to a particular piece of stone.

Tamsin photographed the patch. I wrote down the locations of the old tide marks. Maui held the lamp steady, which helped more than any clever speech would have.

Then the signal sounded from above.

Time to leave.

We climbed carefully and shut the hatch. Danse checked the seal, and Neri recorded the opening in the new access ledger. The public report would include our measurements and photographs without disclosing the private contents of unrelated archive records.

At the square, people were waiting.

Edda had been unable to come down the narrow inspection stairs, so she was listening through the agreed speaking tube while Tamsin described the dimensions. When I repeated the measurement for the third time, Edda interrupted.

"That number doesn't tell me whether someone carrying an inspection case can turn around."

I looked at the tight corner. Maui had moved through it easily. I had, too, though I'd caught my sleeve on the rough mortar.

"No," I said. "It doesn't."

Tamsin measured the clear width, the height of the railing, and the distance from the hatch to the first support. She asked Edda whether a floor plan and a slow walk-through description would help her assess alternative procedures without making her descend a route she couldn't use.

"I can review a plan," Edda said. "And I can tell you which parts still exclude people. But don't write that I inspected a place I couldn't enter."

"Understood."

Danse examined the metal plate bearing the seventh scratch. He found a maker's number beneath the rust, distinct from the scraped signature in the archive. Neither number proved who had ordered the Closed Bells restriction.

"Should we take the plate up?" Maui asked.

"Not yet," Tamsin replied. "We need to photograph how it's attached. Removing it could break a seal we're not authorized to disturb."

Maui lowered his hand from the wall, looking almost embarrassed.

"What can I do?"

"Hold the lamp at the angle I ask for."

He did.

For twenty careful minutes he held it while Fen marked water stains and Neri compared the service drawing to the actual pipe. I kept thinking that in one of his old legends, Maui would have simply lifted the entire wall until the mystery showed itself. Here, the people we'd invited to help would need the wall intact when we were done.

When we finished, Neri checked the access list. Everyone present was accounted for; the tool count matched the one recorded before the hatch opened. Edda asked from above whether we had time left under the safety limit.

"Not much," Danse answered.

"Then tell the heroes to come upstairs."

Maui looked offended until he heard her laugh.

We took the photographs, the measurements, and the unresolved question with us. The locked barrier remained exactly where we'd found it.

"What did you find?" someone called.

"A maintenance chamber and a sealed flood barrier," Tamsin answered.

"Anything magical?"

"Stone, metal, mortar, and an excellent reason to continue inspecting them."

A few people looked disappointed.

I was relieved.

That evening, Maui and I sat beside the sea-glass garden. He held the little brass key in his palm and turned it over.

"I thought it would open something magnificent," he said.

"It opened something important."

"Waterworks?"

"Evidence."

He looked toward the cove.

"Do you ever wish the world would give us an easy answer?"

"All the time."

He took my hand.

The low light caught the scar on his knuckle and the silver along the edge of the key. I moved closer, and he kissed my forehead.

"Did you feel brave down there?" he asked.

"Terrified."

"Me too."

I laughed softly.

The key went back around my neck. The hatch stayed locked until the next authorized inspection.

Above the seventh scratch, travelers passed freely beneath the arch.

Below it, the stone was waiting to be understood.

Neither asked us to become anything other than people willing to ask the right questions.
